home.tagline: A systematic review of how AI learned to generate, arrange and orchestrate music, 2020–2025.
home.summary: This companion site presents the final 107-study corpus from a PRISMA 2020 systematic review of AI music generation, arrangement and orchestration. It extends an existing taxonomy, synthesises eight research trends, and reports a structured listening evaluation of a post-inclusion subset of 29 representative systems — nine of which score 4.0 or above. Everything here is drawn from the dissertation and is browsable independently of the PDF.

aboutThesis.abstract: The rapid growth of AI-based music generation, arrangement and orchestration has produced a large and fragmented literature, making it difficult to navigate recent developments and identify the most promising approaches. This thesis addresses that gap through a systematic literature review following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, covering AI methods published between 2020 and 2025. From 4,521 records identified across six academic databases, 1,083 were transferred to Zotero, 783 unique records remained after deduplication, 383 passed title screening and 146 passed abstract screening. Full-text assessment initially included 113 studies; post-inclusion verification consolidated one duplicate publication version to 112 and reclassified five studies as background, producing the final primary corpus of 107 studies. For each primary study, information on methodology, datasets, musical representations, evaluation procedures, metrics and code availability was extracted into a comprehensive comparison table. The review extends the taxonomy proposed by Zhu et al. (2023), synthesises eight major research trends, and identifies and justifies a post-inclusion subset of 29 representative methods for structured listening analysis.
aboutThesis.aim: To conduct a PRISMA-guided systematic review of AI methods for music generation, arrangement and orchestration, with a focus on developments from 2020 to 2025.
researchQuestions: How have AI-based methods for music generation, arrangement and orchestration evolved since 2020, particularly with the emergence of transformer and diffusion models?
What are the current dominant trends, most commonly used techniques, datasets and evaluation approaches in this field?
Which approaches demonstrate the most promising results, and what factors contribute to their effectiveness?
contributions: An extended taxonomy of AI music systems across four dimensions.
A structured comparison of all 107 verified primary studies.
A synthesis of eight research trends spanning 2020–2025.
A structured listening evaluation of a 29-system post-inclusion subset, presented through a companion website.
objectives: Perform a systematic literature review following PRISMA 2020.
Extend the taxonomy of Zhu et al. (2023) with recent models.
Develop a comparison table of key studies (2020–2025).
Identify and justify the most promising approaches.
Present and analyse selected MIDI/audio examples via an interactive page.
Discuss limitations, challenges and future directions.

systematicReview.title: Systematic review
systematicReview.intro: The review followed the PRISMA 2020 Statement: identification, screening, eligibility assessment, data extraction and qualitative synthesis.

blocks.heading: Data collection
blocks.body: Publications were identified through six databases and digital libraries: Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect and arXiv, using a predefined keyword set. The search yielded 4,521 records; owing to platform export restrictions, 1,083 could be exported to Zotero, and after removing 300 duplicates, 783 unique records remained.

blocks.heading: Study selection
blocks.body: Of the 783 unique records, title screening retained 383 and abstract screening retained 146 for full-text assessment. Full-text eligibility initially included 113 studies. Two post-inclusion verification steps followed: consolidation of the AccoMontage-3 preprint with the published Structured Multi-Track Accompaniment Arrangement contribution reduced the corpus to 112 publication-level studies, and a later eligibility-consistency audit reclassified five studies as background, producing the final primary corpus of 107 studies. These 113→112 and 112→107 transitions document post-inclusion verification rather than rewriting the original PRISMA screening history.

blocks.heading: In-depth subset
blocks.body: After the final 107-study primary corpus was established, 29 systems were selected for in-depth synthesis and listening analysis using five criteria: task coverage (S1), methodological influence (S2), architectural diversity (S3), accessible MIDI/MP3 demonstrations (S4) and temporal spread across 2020–2025 (S5). This is a post-inclusion synthesis subset, not a PRISMA eligibility or exclusion stage; all 107 primary studies remain in the master comparison table.

blocks.heading: Data analysis
blocks.body: For each study, authors, year, task, architecture, dataset, representation, evaluation method, metrics, music length, training requirements and code availability were extracted into the master comparison table and analysed qualitatively to identify trends, dominant methodologies, challenges and future directions.

listeningEvaluation.intro: The 29 selected systems were assessed through manual critical listening on eight dimensions rated on a five-point scale. Each system was judged on at least one representative example — a hosted demo where available, or, where none existed, a locally generated output or the results reported in the paper. As the assessment reflects a single listener, ratings are descriptive summaries rather than objective benchmarks, and where authors publish curated examples they bound the best case rather than the average case.

rubric.label: Audio / rendering quality
rubric.meaning: Cleanliness and fidelity of the produced sound (absence of noise or artefacts).

rubric.label: Melodic coherence
rubric.meaning: Sensibility and sense of direction of the melodic line.

rubric.label: Harmonic coherence
rubric.meaning: Consistency and plausibility of the underlying harmony.

rubric.label: Rhythmic stability
rubric.meaning: Steadiness and regularity of the rhythmic pulse.

rubric.label: Long-term structure
rubric.meaning: Presence of large-scale musical form (e.g. verse–chorus, development).

rubric.label: Control adherence
rubric.meaning: Fidelity of the output to the given conditioning (text, chords, melody or target).

rubric.label: Naturalness / musicality
rubric.meaning: Overall musical plausibility and expressive quality.

rubric.label: Overall
rubric.meaning: Overall judgement integrating the preceding dimensions.

listeningEvaluation.caveat: Scores are descriptive summaries of a structured listening exercise, not objective performance benchmarks, and are interpreted as such throughout.

discussion.intro: The review is interpreted in relation to the three research questions, followed by the limitations of the review and of the field.

rq.q: RQ1 — How have methods evolved since 2020?
rq.a: The corpus describes a three-stage evolution: representation engineering (2020–2022), paradigm competition and the language interface (2023), and consolidation around controllable diffusion, foundation models and evaluation (2024–2025). Transformers supplied the representational substrate and the autoregressive token-LM baseline (Jukebox → AudioLM → MusicGen); diffusion arrived as the complementary paradigm, decisive where autoregression was weakest — global structure and fine-grained control. The two now coexist by a division of labour. In the structured listening subset, the mean overall score was approximately 2.8 in 2020 and approximately 3.9 in 2024; the intervening annual means fluctuate, so this is not a monotonic year-by-year increase.

rq.q: RQ2 — What are the dominant trends, techniques, datasets and evaluation?
rq.a: Eight higher-level trends were synthesised from the 107-study corpus. The largest primary categories are symbolic generation (43 studies) and audio generation (31), followed by arrangement (26) and orchestration (7). The corpus comprises 63 symbolic-domain, 43 audio-domain and one mixed-domain study. Transformer or language-model approaches are most common (40 studies), followed by diffusion (32), VAE (11), hybrid or other (8), GAN (8), RNN/LSTM (5) and flow matching (3). Publication activity is concentrated in 2023 and 2024, which together account for 63 of 107 studies. Evaluation combines objective distributional metrics (notably FAD) with subjective preference and controllability measures, alongside an emerging concern with evaluation validity itself.

rq.q: RQ3 — Which approaches are most promising, and why?
rq.a: Nine of the 29 evaluated methods scored 4.0 or above: GETMusic and ChatMusician (both 4.5), with MusicLM, MusicGen, StemGen, AccoMontage, Whole-Song Generation, Structured Arrangement and SymphonyNet (all 4.0). Two factors separated them: verifiable controllability — the ability to hear that the output follows its conditioning — and explicit long-term structural planning. Audio fidelity was generally high across the subset and did not differentiate the leaders. The most effective systems treated control and structure as first-class design goals rather than by-products of scale.

discussion.limitationsReview: Screening was carried out by a single reviewer, introducing a risk of selection bias. Export restrictions on three databases meant only 1,083 of 4,521 records could be exported, so the screened set is broad but not exhaustive. The auditory analysis reflects a single listener and is indicative rather than statistically generalisable; where authors publish curated examples, the ratings bound the best case, and for systems without a public demonstration the assessment relied on reported results.
discussion.limitationsField: Evaluation validity emerged as one of the most pressing challenges: distributional metrics correlate imperfectly with human judgement, and some reported gains do not survive fair comparison. Cultural bias is a second concern, as models trained predominantly on Western music generalise poorly beyond those idioms. Efficiency and latency remain obstacles to interactive use. Two capability gaps recur: convincing sung vocals were absent from every system evaluated, and genuine long-term structure remained difficult except where explicitly planned.

futureDirections.title: Future directions
futureDirections.intro: The results point to several concrete directions, grounded in the review rather than in generic future-work statements.

blocks.heading: The orchestration gap
blocks.body: Orchestration is the least-served task in the corpus, plausibly because it lacks the large paired datasets that fuelled generation research and because instrument interdependence and timbre resist simple tokenisation. Building such datasets and adapting foundation models to orchestration and arrangement is a promising, under-explored direction.

blocks.heading: Controllable long-form structure
blocks.body: The hierarchical and two-stage planning that proved most effective here should be extended toward reliably controllable long-form structure.

blocks.heading: Preference-aligned objectives
blocks.body: Carrying the reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback turn further into music generation could align outputs with listener preference rather than likelihood.

blocks.heading: Standardised evaluation
blocks.body: Improved, standardised evaluation that better reflects human musical judgement and addresses cultural coverage would strengthen the field's claims.

blocks.heading: Sung vocals
blocks.body: Progress on convincing, intelligible singing — the field's most visible remaining frontier — would broaden applicability beyond instrumental music.

glossary.definition: A standard set of guidelines for transparent reporting of systematic reviews, covering identification, screening, eligibility and synthesis.
Music represented as notes or scores (e.g. MIDI, ABC notation) rather than raw sound.
Music represented as raw waveform or spectrogram/codec tokens rather than symbolic notes.
An autoregressive Transformer language model over music tokens — the dominant neural paradigm across the corpus.
A generative model that synthesises output by iteratively denoising, offering whole-context generation and step-by-step conditioning.
A variational autoencoder — a latent-variable model used for structured, controllable representations.
A system built on a general-purpose pretrained large language model adapted to read and write music.
A large model pretrained at scale and reused across tasks, rather than a task-specific architecture.
A generative training objective, positioned as a successor to diffusion, often at lower parameter cost.
A linear-time sequence backbone offered as an alternative to the Transformer for long sequences.
Generating a backing or accompaniment for a given lead, rather than a whole piece from scratch.
Deciding which instruments play what — from timbre matching to controllable re-orchestration.
How faithfully a system's output follows its conditioning (text, chords, melody or target).
Large-scale musical form such as verse–chorus organisation or thematic development.
Fréchet Audio Distance — a common objective metric comparing generated audio to a reference distribution.

domain.Symbolic: Music as notes or score (MIDI, ABC notation).
domain.Audio: Music as raw waveform or audio/codec tokens.
domain.Mixed: A system spanning both symbolic and audio representations.

task.Symbolic generation: Generating music represented as notes or score.
task.Audio generation: Generating music represented as waveform or audio tokens.
task.Arrangement: Backing or accompaniment for a given lead.
task.Orchestration: Choosing instruments; timbre matching or re-orchestration.

paradigm.Transformer: Autoregressive Transformer language model over music tokens.
paradigm.LLM: A repurposed general-purpose large language model.
paradigm.Foundation model: Large model pretrained at scale and reused across tasks.
paradigm.Diffusion: Iterative denoising generation with step-by-step conditioning.
paradigm.Flow matching: A flow-based generative objective, successor to diffusion.
paradigm.State-space: Linear-time sequence backbone (Mamba) alternative to the Transformer.
paradigm.Non-neural: Rules, search or optimisation rather than a neural generator.
